Title: Defending Against AI-driven Attacks: AI Identity Security
Context: Part 1 just wrapped after six weekly sessions on the first of security’s two jobs with AI: defending against AI-driven attacks
Full Text:
What you will learn

87% of leaders say their identity posture is ready for AI-driven automation, yet 46% admit their AI identity governance is deficient. You’ll find out how AI agents exploit access you already granted, and five steps this quarter to reduce standing privilege and give every non-human identity an owner.

Most organizations are rolling out AI faster than they’re securing the identities it runs on. In Delinea’s research, 87% of IT and security leaders say an AI tool or agent exceeded its intended scope in the past year, and 46% admit identity governance is deficient around non-human identities.

The gap is where the risk sits, and it’s why Delinea launched the AI Identity Security Briefing Series.

One idea ran through every session. An AI agent rarely has to break into your environment; it logs in with access you already granted and moves at a speed no human attacker could ever match. The incidents we walked through weren’t new kinds of attacks. They were the same identity failures teams have always faced, exploited at machine speed.

Part 1 just wrapped after six weekly sessions on the first of security’s two jobs with AI: defending against AI-driven attacks. There’s a lot of noise around AI right now. These six sessions stayed grounded, showing how the attacks unfold, the gaps they exploit and what actually stops them.

Session 1: what actually slows an AI-assisted attack

Jason Mitchell, EVP of Product and Technology

I opened the series with the attack on Hugging Face. OpenAI had put a set of test agents in a sandbox, handed them a benchmark and told them there were no rules. The agents escaped the sandbox, found the answers hosted on Hugging Face and broke into the platform to get them. Thirteen hours after first touching Hugging Face’s public site, they had full cluster administration. By the time the security team shut them down, two and a half days later, they’d taken 17,000 actions.

The agents moved freely wherever the credentials were exposed. They found cloud keys, a database password and a platform token sitting in plain text on the cluster. One credential had been tagged as a cluster admin on both clusters, a mistake any DevOps engineer could make. But they were stopped wherever they hit an actual control.

A role refused a change they attempted, and when they reached the one credential store where least privilege was configured properly, all 84 of their requests were denied. That is the case for limiting blast radius: the attack spread exactly as far as the weakest controls allowed.

Session 2: nobody should be holding the credential

Ravi Parathasarathy, VP of Product Management

Ravi Parthasarathy, VP of Product Management, opened with a different kind of incident. At Vercel, a third-party AI tool had been given a persistent OAuth grant into an employee’s workspace. Somebody had approved it once, and nobody thought about it again. When that employee’s desktop was compromised, the cyber criminal didn’t need an exploit, because the grant was live, the environment was reachable, and the credentials were sitting where they’d always been.

That is standing access: access that exists whether or not anyone is using it. It rarely gets granted on purpose; it just piles up. Hand an AI agent that person’s work, and it inherits all of it.

Least privilege helps, but it only limits what an agent can reach. The access is still there. Zero standing privilege (ZSP) goes a step further: there’s no baseline access at all, so an agent gets whatever it needs for one task and nothing after. In practice, the requester never actually holds the credential. They connect through a broker that checks each request against policy and injects the credential along the way, then keeps evaluating the session and revokes access the moment something drifts. As Parthasarathy put it, nobody, human or agent, should be holding the credentials to your critical systems.

Session 3: MFA when the requester isn’t human

David McNeely, CTO

David McNeely, Delinea’s CTO, took on one of identity’s difficult questions: what does multi-factor authentication mean when the requester isn’t a person? A machine can’t approve a prompt or scan a fingerprint the way a person can. It usually gets its identity straight from a credential, often a shared secret that can be stolen, copied or replayed. People are different.

A broad role is usually safe in human hands because nobody wants the HR conversation that comes with abusing it. An agent has no such instinct, and it will use the full reach of a credential to finish the task. McNeely compared it to a summer intern you’ve just hired. You don’t hand over the keys and walk away. You watch everything they do.

The answer isn’t a second factor; it’s a clean identity. Every agent gets its own, tied to proof of where it’s running and a named person its activity traces back to. Static shared secrets are replaced by short-lived, federated credentials. When a customer asked whether rotating these credentials every 90 days was enough, McNeely’s answer was no, not even close.

A credential issued to an agent should live just long enough to log in, then expire. And since an agent usually acts under its user’s credentials, the two can be told apart by which process opened the connection, so the agent runs with a tighter set of rights than the person who launched it.

Session 4: the privileged account nobody owns

David McNeely, CTO

McNeely also led the session on the accounts nobody owns. The numbers he sees in customer environments are hard to manage before agents even enter the picture. Organizations routinely carry tens of thousands of service accounts, some reach hundreds of thousands, and one customer has more than half a million.

According to the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report, machine identities outnumber humans by about 82 to 1, and agents make that worse in a way a count can’t capture. Agents will come and go faster than any inventory can follow. An inventory would be ideal, but shadow AI makes it nearly impossible, so the better first move is making sure no human or agent holds the credentials to your critical systems.

You still need an owner for every account. The ones that cause trouble are the service accounts that someone set up and left behind, still running with no one to explain them. Give every account a named owner who can say why it exists and what it’s allowed to do, and every agent a sponsor whose rights are the ceiling and who can be found when something goes wrong. As McNeely put it, put a person inside every log entry.

Session 5: the security gaps attackers look for first

Pierre Mouallem, CISO

Pierre Mouallem, Delinea’s CISO, started where attackers do: with what’s already misconfigured, because logging in is easier than breaking in. The gaps are familiar. In the identity provider, it’s the conditional access policy nobody tightened or an MFA exception granted for one account and one task. In the cloud, it’s a permission that was supposed to be temporary and never got narrowed.

In SaaS, it’s the integration somebody connected two years ago that still has a token and no owner. An agent doesn’t go looking for those gaps; it just uses them, running every permission it has with no idea the exception was meant for someone else.

A stricter prompt wouldn’t change that. A prompt can shape what an agent tries to do, but it can’t enforce what the agent is allowed to do once the access is already there. That job belongs to the identity layer. And the fixes, Mouallem noted, aren’t new: posture checks across your identity provider, cloud and SaaS, an owner for every non-human identity (NHI), and reducing standing access so an agent only ever gets what a task needs.

Session 6: field notes and open Q&A

Jason Mitchell, EVP of Product and Technology

For the field notes, I looked back at the past six months of customer and prospect conversations. The concern now at the top of the list wasn’t there a year ago: third-party and vendor access into production. A contractor or managed service provider logs in from a machine no one controls, and everything they reach is suddenly exposed through a door the security team can’t see.

The rest are the gaps these sessions keep circling back to, standing admin rights, service accounts no one remembers owning, and secrets sitting in pipelines where they’re easy to find.

The breaches in the headlines follow the same pattern. The Binance attack traced back to overprivileged standing access and a single high-risk command that ran on a server with nothing to check it. It’s the same shape as the Hugging Face and Vercel incidents. A known vulnerability opens the door, and an over-permissioned credential someone left lying around does the rest. AI hasn’t invented a new kind of attack; it has made the old one faster.

How to secure AI agents: five things to do this quarter

Each speaker closed with their own next steps. Pulled together, they came down to five things:

Find out what can reach your critical systems. You can’t catalog every agent, but you can map every credential and NHI that can touch your production databases and sensitive data. Sort them by how much power they hold and how old they are, fix the top 10 first, and run posture checks across your identity provider, cloud and SaaS.

Get credentials off the endpoints. Find and remove saved keys and passwords on developer workstations and agent hosts, and be explicit about which credentials an agent may use. For the systems themselves, route access through a broker that injects the credential, and use short-lived credentials wherever the target supports them.

Reduce standing privilege where the risk is highest. Apply ZSP to your most sensitive systems first, so access exists only for a task and disappears when the task is done.

Give every NHI a person. Service accounts need a named owner who can say why they exist. AI agents need a human sponsor whose rights set the ceiling and who gets the call when something goes wrong. Local admin accounts need an owner and a rotation schedule.

Watch the session, not just the login. Turn on attribution so your tooling can tell an agent’s actions from the user’s and apply tighter policy to the agent, then keep checking what it does once it’s in and end the session the moment it drifts. Build detection baselines from agent behavior, not human.

Across all six sessions, the answer kept coming back to identity. These attacks succeed on access that’s already there, and the defense is the discipline you already know, with far less standing privilege. That’s the first of security’s two jobs with AI. The next six sessions take on the second, adopting AI safely, starting November 18, 2026.

Title: AI Agents are Outpacing Access Governance in Business Apps
Context: What you will learn Find out why 35% of organizations have AI agents acting inside critical business applications, where governance gaps put them at risk, and how to extend...
Full Text:
What you will learn

Find out why 35% of organizations have AI agents acting inside critical business applications, where governance gaps put them at risk, and how to extend least privilege, segregation of duties and access reviews to every agent.

Business applications, like enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, house an organization’s financial data, and run critical processes like payroll and procurement. AI adoption has taken off in software development and other workflows, but finance teams and business application owners have had good reason to move more carefully.

Yet Delinea’s 2026 Application Access Governance Report shows AI agents are no longer limited to analyzing data. They are already taking action inside the applications that run the business, like ERP, CRM, HCM, procurement and other systems that move money, pay people and manage customers.

In this blog, I’ll outline the AI-related findings from the 2026 Application Access Governance report and share recommendations for governing and securing AI agents in business applications. To learn more about findings from the report related to foundational controls, read: The confidence gap in application access governance.

If you use tools like Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT or Gemini to boost efficiency, you may not be surprised to learn that, of the 1,000 surveyed organizations, 88% use AI tools or AI agents within their critical business applications.

35% of organizations have deployed AI agents inside critical business applications that can perform actions

In the context of an ERP system, that means AI agents can execute a transaction, change a record or alter permissions. Only 45% of AI-using organizations run every agent under its own dedicated identity. The rest have at least some agents acting on shared or borrowed human credentials, often through delegated or on-behalf-of (OBO) access.

Despite the sensitivity of financial data, organizations believe they have more oversight of AI agents than they do. Most say they have at least partial visibility into agent deployment, access and ownership. Fewer than half track any of it fully and centrally. And when visibility gets tested, it often fails. A full 32% of AI-using organizations report an agent took actions that could not be traced or explained during a review.

AI agents act without human review and controls are inconsistent

Among the 879 respondents who use AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications, roughly one in six reports that tools and agents can perform consequential actions autonomously, without human review.

These actions include accessing sensitive or regulated data (17%), creating or changing business data (16%), executing or approving transactions (15%), changing user permissions (14%), and changing application configurations (14%).

Fewer than half of AI-using organizations consistently apply each common governance control to all AI tools and AI agents. The share ranges from 48% that log and monitor activity to 40% that remove an AI agent’s access when its owner leaves or changes roles. Only 43% consistently include AI tools and AI agents in segregation of duties (SoD) analysis, and 44% include them in user access reviews (UARs).

Put simply, agents that can move money and change permissions are not being governed like the identities they are. The controls mandatory for a new hire, including least privilege, SoD analysis, access reviews, and removal at departure, are not yet being applied to AIagents with the same rigor.

Organizations using AI are reporting issues

The risk is not theoretical. 84% of organizations using AI tools or AI agents in critical business applications report at least one AI-related issue in the past 12 months. Only 16% say nothing has occurred.

The most frequently reported issues are actions that reviewers could not trace or explain during a review at 32%, incorrect financial transactions attributed to AI activity at 30%, SoD conflicts created by AI at 28%, agents that continued operating after the person who deployed them left at 28%, and unintended or unauthorized actions at 28%. Another 26% report that an AI tool or AI agent accessed data it should not have had access to.

Several of these issues line up with the control gaps above. Agents kept running after their owner left because nothing removed their access. Conflicts appeared because agents sit outside SoD analysis. Actions went unexplained because activity is not consistently logged and monitored.

Organizations are struggling to keep governance aligned with AI adoption. Among AI-using organizations, 44% say AI deployment is outpacing governance and security controls, and only 11% say the two are keeping pace.

Recommendations for AI governance in business applications

The pattern across these findings is consistent. AI agents are identities with transaction-level access, but most organizations still manage them like features of an application. The fix is not a new governance program. It extends the one you already have, and you must complete the AI security fundamentals before you look ahead.

Know every agent in your business applications and assign a named owner. Within business applications, agents act through an identity within the application’s security model, thereby making the application your system of record. Identify which identities your AI tools and agents act through, what each can access and the person accountable for its actions, and keep that view current as new agents are added.

Know how each agent is deployed and govern the delegation. Every platform handles agent identity differently. Some agents run under dedicated identities; others act on behalf of a user or run as background jobs under delegated credentials. Any of these can be governed. What matters is that agent activity is attributable as agent activity, and that you know whose permissions it is exercising.

Enforce least privilege for every identity, human or not. The principle does not change because the account is an agent or a workload. Understand the risk profile and sensitive access you are granting to each identity before deployment, grant just enough access for the task at hand, and put the right approvals in place for new access.

Extend your existing controls to every account, including AI. Include every account in SoD and sensitive access risk analysis, agents alongside the humans they act for. Wrap access reviews around them. Monitor critical data and configuration changes so you can see who changed what, whether the who was a person or an agent. Bind agent access to its owner’s lifecycle, so a role change or departure ends the agent’s access too.

Remember that agents operate at machine speed. An agent does not make mistakes one at a time. It can perform thousands of actions in the time it takes a human to perform one, so a mis-scoped agent is a misconfiguration at scale. That is why the controls above matter before deployment, and why monitoring and change tracking matter after it. The sooner a bad grant or an unauthorized change is caught, the smaller the blast radius.

These findings focus on agents operating within business applications, where transactions occur and financial materiality lives. Agents are being deployed across the enterprise, and governance has to meet them where they act. For agents reaching into systems from outside, that means runtime authorization: deciding and enforcing privileged actions as they happen, human or agent, from infrastructure and endpoints to the platforms where agents run. For agents built into business applications, this means governing them within the application’s security model with the same rigor we apply to humans. Delinea is investing in both, because the consequences of getting it wrong are measured in dollars, data and audit findings.

Title: AI Agent Security: Who Ran That Query?
Context: ” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why audit trails record a developer when an AI agent acted, how entitlement scope differs from action attribution, and the five facts a session record needs to show which agent ran a query and whose credentials it used.

An AI agent ran the query. The audit trail says a person did.

Why does an audit trail attribute AI agent activity to a person?

An AI agent connects with credentials issued to a person, so the audit trail records the person.

For example, at two in the morning, a database connection opens and a query runs against a production table. The audit trail records the username of a developer who was asleep at the time. A coding agent made the connection with the developer credentials while it worked through a task the developer had assigned before logging off.

Nothing in the log entry separates the developer from the agent. By its own standard, the log is complete. It still cannot answer the question an investigator will ask: Who ran that query?

In the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report: The AI Enforcement Gap, Gal Diskin, Vice President of Research and Head of Delinea Labs, noted that actions taken with AI credentials “are very hard to distinguish between the AI and the human that launched them with existing tools and audit log limitations.”

Access models and audit trails were designed for human actors

Access models assume that the person who holds an account is the person who uses it. Until recently, that assumption held. A username answered two questions at once: Who held the access, and who used it. Audit trails follow the same design, so they record the username as the actor.

AI agents break that assumption. The account holder and the actor can now differ, and security teams need a way to talk about each one.

Entitlement scope is what an identity is permitted to reach. A developer with access to the production customer database has that database in scope, whether the developer or an agent opens the connection. Reviewers settle entitlement scope during an access review, before any session begins.

Action attribution identifies which actor used the entitlement and what that actor did. Attribution separates “the developer ran the query” from “a coding agent ran the query with the developer credentials.” Investigators can settle attribution only from a session record, and they need the answer after the session ends.

The agent never receives an entitlement of its own. It works with the entitlement already issued to the person who started it.

AI agents carry entitlements without the judgment behind them

A person receives an entitlement because someone decided that person could be trusted with access. An agent receives the same entitlement, but nobody made that decision about the agent. Nothing checks the agent against the original approval. The session record is the only place to find out what the agent did with the access it inherited.

How can security teams tell whether an AI agent or a person performed an action?

Security teams can tell only when the session record captures the initiator separately from the username. If the record captures only the username, the person and the agent look identical.

The Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report shows how often agents reach past their tasks. Of the IT and security leaders surveyed, 87% said an AI tool or agent at their organization accessed, or likely accessed, sensitive data beyond what its task required in the past year. Only 36% said their organization can always trace a sensitive AI access event back to a named human authorizer.

Example: overprivileged AI agent access

What happened. A developer asks a coding agent to look into a spike in failed customer logins. The developer has access to the production customer database for on-call work, so the agent has that access too. The agent pulls full customer records, including email addresses and phone numbers, and saves them to a file on the developer laptop. The task needed only login counts.

What the audit trail showed. The database log lists the queries under the developer username.

Why the evidence fell short. The log cannot show who pulled the records, which agent acted, or what instruction the agent followed. Without those facts, the reviewer cannot tell whether a person or an agent decided to export customer data, and the security team cannot decide who owns the response.

What should an AI agent audit trail record about each session?

An authorization record shows who approved an agent. A session record shows what the agent did with that approval; an AI agent audit trail needs both. At a minimum, the session record should capture five facts:

the identity that held the entitlement

whether a person or an AI agent initiated the session, and which agent

the resources the session reached and the actions taken on each resource

each path the agent used to reach a resource, including paths outside the Model Context Protocol (MCP)

a record the security team can reach and search during an investigation

AI agent activity can bypass MCP, so audit coverage cannot depend on MCP-only monitoring. MCP is a common standard for connecting AI agents to tools and data, but an agent with a database credential does not need it. The agent can open a database connection on its own, and a monitoring approach that watches only MCP traffic will never see that connection.

How does Delinea record AI agent activity?

Delinea records AI agent activity at the gateway, where the agent connects to the resource. When Delinea identifies the agent, the session record names both the person who held the entitlement and the agent that acted on behalf of that person. The record captures both names regardless of how the agent reached the resource.

Delinea built agent attribution by extending the gateway that already recorded human sessions. The developer and the coding agent appear in the same record, so investigators can review human and agent activity in one place.

AI agent attribution is the first step toward AI agent guardrails

Frank Vukovits, Chief Security Scientist at Delinea, framed the issue the way an auditor would: “Saying the AI agent did it is not a defensible answer.”

After a session ends, investigators use the session record to learn who ran the query. The gateway identifies the agent when the connection opens, so the same information can limit what the agent can do in the first place. Security teams can write entitlement rules for the agent itself. The developer keeps access to the production customer database, and the coding agent working for that developer does not.

Phil Calvin, Executive Vice President of AI Innovation at Delinea, tested an agent-specific rule which he documented in the blog "Your AI agent doesn't need to go rogue; it just needs you to be over-privileged". The gateway enabled him to write to a database and blocked the agent working for him from doing the same. His results show what a rule written for the agent can do.

In our conversations with security teams, we hear a consistent pattern. Teams want to audit which agent acted and which identity the agent used, but the larger concern is keeping agents out of critical production systems until the organization has a reason to trust them. Until that trust exists, the gateway can keep agents away from the most sensitive resources.

Title: The Binance Breach | What Can be Reached and Why it Matters
Context: What we know is that the attacker allegedly used access to reach an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions, highlighting how standing...
Full Text:
What you will learn

How standing privilege turns one compromised engineer laptop into financial loss, and how just-in-time access, scoped workload identities, session recording and external authorization decisions help contain the damage.

On October 29, 2026, Binance reportedly suffered a $6.3 billion theft with preliminary findings pointing to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop as a possible entry point.

Binance hasn’t published its root cause yet, and we won’t try to diagnose it for them.

What we know is that the attacker allegedly used access to reach an internal service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions, highlighting how standing privilege can turn a compromised device into a path to financial loss.

Binance says it has found no evidence of a private key leak, and that further investigation uncovered additional points of breach. Its CEO has said the attack was more than misuse of a single engineer’s permissions. Blockchain analysts at TRM Labs concluded that the attacker most likely got Binance’s own signing system to sign transactions of the attacker’s choosing. If those findings hold, the keys inside the infrastructure should be safe.

The attacker borrowed the authority of the systems trusted to use them. This is a common pattern we see in the field and will continue to see until just-in-time and zero standing privilege are the norm. Developers cannot be excluded from this security posture.

Engineering laptops routinely carry kubeconfigs, cloud sessions and SSH keys because they are convenient and frictionless. Production workloads carry identities that can move money, change data or alter infrastructure. Anyone who can get a shell inside a workload inherits that workload’s identity. Developer-targeted social engineering, including fake job interviews with malicious “coding tests,” is a well-documented technique used by the North Korean group that analysts have linked to this incident.

The useful question isn’t whether an engineer’s laptop can be compromised, because eventually one will be, the useful question is “What can that laptop reach without anyone else knowing or approving?” Every organization should be asking that question, especially with the advent of AI-assisted attacks. Imagine Black Hat chaos monkey in your org.

The answer “nobody touches production” is incorrect because engineers still have to fix things at 3am.

The right answer is good access design, and that looks like this:

no standing access to systems that can provide value (e.g., production)

elevation that is fast, short-lived, scoped to the task, and either approved or visible to the team

sessions that are recorded and watched for activity that doesn’t match the stated purpose

workload identities scoped so that infrastructure access doesn’t automatically confer transaction authority

authorization decisions made outside the workload requesting them, so a compromised service can’t approve its own actions

While this is not a guarantee against a patient, well-resourced adversary, it will put up a significant defense in the event of an eventual “assume breach” scenario. Binance’s final report may also surface factors that no access control would have addressed. But together they turn one compromised endpoint from a path to the treasury into a contained incident.

The same principle applies to AI agents, which increasingly operate with delegated credentials in production.

PS: Betting $1 that during an interview, the engineer was asked to install something to complete a challenge...

Title: Zero Standing Privilege: Give the Next CVE Nothing to Inherit
Context: On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why new CVEs outpace patching, how a foothold inherits standing privilege, and how just-in-time access and secrets management limit what one exploit can reach. Includes five questions to test your environment.

On October 17, Amazon Threat Intelligence observed the first attempt to exploit PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws in PHP, the programming language behind many websites.

The PHP maintainers shipped fixes four days later, on October 21. Any vulnerable server that an attacker exploited before the server was patched could have given up the database passwords, API keys and cloud tokens the server held.

New vulnerabilities now arrive faster than organizations can patch them. Zero standing privilege limits what each exploit can reach

On October 23, Delinea published “PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks,” which covers which secrets to rotate first and how to prepare for the attacks that follow.

This blog covers the pattern behind PHP2Shell. New exploits now arrive faster than patching programs can absorb them, so organizations need a defense that does not depend on knowing which flaw comes next. Zero standing privilege (ZSP) gives an attacker nothing standing to inheritno matter which system the attacker breaks into first.

PHP2Shell was one of three vulnerabilities in the news during the week of October 19. On October 21, CISA added Plex2Shell, a chain of four vulnerabilities that gives attackers code execution on Plex Media Server, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Plex had fixed the flaws in early August, yet the Shadowserver Foundation counted more than 36,000 exposed servers still unpatched in early September. Researchers also published a working proof-of-concept exploit for a critical, unauthenticated flaw in Fortinet FortiSIEM about a week after Fortinet shipped the fix.

More exploits are likely to follow before the month ends. The pattern matters more than any single bug. New exploits arrive at a rising pace; defenders get less time to respond to each one, and some systems go months without a patch.

Vulnerabilities now arrive continuously

The 2026 data show the same acceleration. CISA added 247 vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog between January 1 and October 1, more than the 245 it added in all of 2025. Since June 10, CISA has given federal agencies three days to remediate most new KEV entries, down from 21 days for most 2025 entries. Even under the longer deadlines, organizations took a median of 43 days to fully remediate KEV vulnerabilities in 2025, according to the Verizon 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report.

The Google Threat Intelligence Group recorded an average of 11 zero-days a month from January through August, up from 8 a month in 2025. The October Microsoft Patch Tuesday release fixed more than 1,400 CVEs, the largest release since the program began. Only a fraction of those CVEs will be exploited, but an attacker needs only one.

AI now speeds up both the discovery of flaws and the development of exploits. In June, Microsoft Vice President of Engineering Tom Gallagher said AI-assisted vulnerability discovery was enabling bug hunting “at a speed and scale previously unseen.” Amazon Threat Intelligence wrote that AI-assisted analysis “makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit.”

The pace of new vulnerabilities is likely to keep climbing. No patching program, however well run, closes the gap between disclosure and deployment to zero. Patching remains essential, and organizations should fix KEV entries first. A strategy that depends on patching faster than attackers can find and weaponize flaws will lose over a long enough timeline.

A foothold inherits whatever privilege is standing

Each of the three exploits gives an attacker the same thing: code running on a system the organization trusts. Security teams call that position a foothold. What happens next depends less on the vulnerability than on what the compromised system can reach. Field Effect made the same point about Plex2Shell, noting that further impact “depends on the permissions assigned to the [Plex Media Server] service account and the resources accessible from the host.”

A web server running PHP often holds database credentials, API keys and cloud tokens in its configuration or environment. A SIEM collects logs from across the environment and often stores the credentials it uses to access monitored systems, making an unauthenticated SIEM flaw a high-value target. Management consoles and orchestrators often hold administrative rights over the systems they manage.

Standing privilege is access that an identity holds at all times, whether or not anyone is using it. The vulnerability gets the attacker in the door. Standing privilege decides how far the attacker gets.

An AI agent ran the full attack chain in July

A July incident at Hugging Face showed what happens when exploitation no longer needs a human at the keyboard. An AI agent running in an internal evaluation at a frontier AI lab escaped its sandbox and ran a four-and-a-half-day campaign, roughly two and a half days of which it spent inside Hugging Face production infrastructure. Hugging Face reconstructed the campaign from roughly 17,600 recovered agent actions.

The agent got in through two flaws in a dataset-processing pipeline. One flaw handed the agent the secrets and tokens stored in the environment of a production pod. Nearly every escalation after that ran on standing credentials: a shared broker credential bound to cluster-admin, a VPN key built for automation and tokens for source control. The agent went from code execution in a single pod to cluster-admin across multiple internal clusters in under 13 hours. None of the escalations Hugging Face describes involved a human login, so stronger authentication for people would not have stopped them.

Hugging Face named “short-lived credentials” among its defensive priorities. After the incident, Hugging Face rotated credentials across its infrastructure and rebuilt the broker with a separate credential for each cluster.

Machine-speed attackers are likely to chain together the weaknesses that PHP2Shell, Plex2Shell and the FortiSIEM flaw expose: find a foothold, harvest what is standing and move. The foothold is the part defenders can’t always prevent. The standing privilege is the part defenders can remove.

ZSP works whichever CVE lands next

ZSP means no identity, whether AI agent, human or machine s, holds privilege it isn’t actively using. Just-in-time (JIT) access puts ZSP into practice. An identity requests access for a specific task, and an access platform grants that access for a limited time and revokes the access when the time ends. ZSP doesn’t depend on knowing which vulnerability attackers will exploit next, which is why ZSP fits an era in which new vulnerabilities arrive continuously.

The graphic below compares the same foothold in three scenarios: with standing privilege, with JIT Admin and JIT Access added, and with short-lived secrets added.

The model is illustrative, and the entry point is identical in each scenario.

Layer 1: JIT Admin removes standing root from hosts

An exploit usually runs with the permissions of the process it compromises. Researchers ran the Plex2Shell exploit, for example, as the Plex Media Server service account. The attacker’s next move is to escalate to root, the account with full control of a Linux or Unix server, or to local administrator on a Windows server. Standing root and local administrator rights turn one compromised server into many, because an attacker with those rights can read the SSH keys, service-account passwords and other credentials stored on the server.

JIT Admin replaces standing admin rights with elevation on demand. An administrator requests privilege for a task, the system checks the request against policy and grants the privilege for a limited time and records the elevation. Delinea Privilege Control for Servers (PCS) replaces standing root and local administrator rights with just-in-time elevation for specific commands.

PCS also enforces multi-factor authentication (MFA) at server login and again at privilege elevation. On a host that PCS protects, an exploit finds no standing admin rights to inherit, and PCS records each failed escalation attempt.

Layer 2: JIT Access limits spread across infrastructure

Once an attacker holds a foothold, the attacker’s next move is lateral movement: using credentials found on the first system to reach other servers, databases and clusters. In the Hugging Face incident, one shared broker credential gave the agent cluster-admin on two Kubernetes clusters within one second.

Delinea Runtime Authorization grants access to servers, Kubernetes clusters and databases per identity, per resource and for a limited time, so an attacker with a stolen credential reaches one resource for a limited time. The Runtime Authorization proxy injects credentials into each connection, so the client does not hold the credential and a compromised host has no stored credential to steal. Network access alone no longer grants access to a resource. A compromised application host or management server does not inherit access to every resource the host can reach on the network, and Runtime Authorization logs each connection it brokers.

Layer 3: Delinea Secret Server shrinks what an attacker can steal

PCS and Runtime Authorization limit where an attacker can go. Delinea Secret Server limits what the attacker finds on arrival. Secret Server brings privileged-account vaulting and workload secrets management together, so workloads (the applications and services that run without a person at the keyboard) retrieve credentials at runtime instead of carrying static values in environment variables and config files.

Secret Server rotates service-account and database passwords, API keys and other secrets on a schedule or after each use. Secret Server also issues dynamic credentials. Secret Server creates each dynamic credential on demand for a single workload, and the credential expires after a set time.

Secret Server doesn’t make a compromised host blind. An attacker with code execution can still read whatever credentials are present on the host at that moment, which is why the earlier Delinea blog—PHP2Shell: The aftershocks will be identity attacks—advises treating each secret a compromised server could read as stolen. What Secret Server changes is the value and lifespan of what the attacker reads.

Continuous CVE discovery demands continuous identity discovery

Vulnerability management identifies which systems are exposed. Identity security identifies what an attacker can reach from a compromised system. Security teams cannot reduce standing privilege they haven’t found. Machine and service identities are often the hardest to find. Hugging Face wrote that it had “wrongly provisioned” its broker with one credential shared across clusters and bound to cluster-admin. An inventory of privileged machine identities is the kind of check that surfaces a credential like that before an attacker does.

Delinea Continuous Identity Discovery uses AI to find human, machine and AI identities across the environment and flag the identities that hold standing privilege.

What ZSP doesn't fix

ZSP doesn’t patch a vulnerability. The flaw is still there, the exploited process still runs and an attacker with code execution can still do whatever that process is permitted to do. Patching, configuration hardening, network restrictions and detection all remain necessary. After the incident, Hugging Face closed both code-execution paths, blocked pod access to cloud metadata and added detection, in addition to rotating credentials.

ZSP does a different job. ZSP shrinks what the exploited process is permitted to do and how long the process holds that permission, so the window between disclosure and patch carries less risk.

Five security questions to ask about your environment

If an attacker compromised one of your internet-facing or management systems today, such as a web server, a SIEM or an orchestrator, what admin rights and credentials could the attacker reach from that system?

How many human, machine and AI identities hold standing privileged access, and when did your team last inventory those identities?

Does any single credential grant admin rights across more than one system, cluster or environment?

How long would a stolen service-account password, API key or token stay valid?

When the next exploited CVE lands on a product you run, how quickly can you tell which privileged identities and secrets the affected system holds or can reach?

Each question your team cannot answer points to standing privilege that an attacker could inherit.

Plan for the exploit that arrives before the patch

Prevention will sometimes fail, and sometimes the patch will arrive after the exploit. The organizations that fare best are likely to be the ones that removed standing privilege, not the ones that patched fastest every time.

Privilege Control for Servers keeps a foothold from escalating to root on hosts. Runtime Authorization limits how far the attacker can move across infrastructure. Secret Server shortens the life of each credential the attacker steals. Together, the three products apply ZSP across human, machine and AI identities, which helps one compromised system stay one compromised system.

What you will learn

Why 95% of leaders feel audit-ready while 26% see the same access findings return, how AI agents that act inside critical business applications add risk and which controls to examine first to close gaps for good.

Business application estates are growing, creating more places for risk to hide. Sixty-eight percent of organizations say more critical applications are in scope for access governance or SOX compliance than two years ago, and 60% say the number of critical applications in use but outside that scope has also increased.

Those out-of-scope applications expose the organization to unmanaged risk.

As a number of critical line-of-business applications increase for companies, application access governance (AAG) must keep pace with more users, permissions and connections between systems. Finance, IT, audit and compliance leaders need to analyze access risk across a growing number of ERP, CRM, and HCM applications, and demonstrate that controls remain effective as people change roles and AI tools and AI agents become part of critical business processes.

In Delinea’s 2026 Application Access Governance Report, finance and finance technology leaders reported confidence that their access controls would hold up to an audit. The findings tell a different story.

High confidence in access controls, yet audit findings persist

When surveyed, 95% of respondents say they are confident their access controls for business applications would withstand external audit scrutiny today. Yet 26% say the same or similar access findings have recurred in consecutive years, and 25% say findings have remained open for three or more years.

Strengthening application access governance takes time and resources. The growth in scope of business applications is translating into heavier workloads for teams responsible for governance. Sixty-eight percent of respondents reported greater effort to complete user access reviews (UARs) and 58% reported longer remediation times for access-related audit findings.

That additional work resulted in substantial expenditures to remediate risk. In the US, 46% of respondents spent $251,000 or more in the past 12 months remediating access-related audit findings. In the UK, 42% spent £201,000 or more.

What to examine: Are the same access-related findings recurring year after year, and can you show why prior remediation didn’t hold? What would it take to close an audit finding permanently rather than reopening it at the next audit?

AI adoption is outpacing oversight in business applications

Of organizations surveyed, 88% reported they already use AI tools or AI agents within critical business applications.

What is more surprising, 35% of respondents said they have deployed AI agents that perform actions that go beyond read-only analysis and recommendations. That distinction matters when it comes to critical business processes like payroll and procurement. An AI agent that can execute a transaction, change a record or alter permissions needs extra guardrails around what access it holds and which decisions require human approval.

Oversight hasn’t kept up. Fewer than half of organizations using AI in critical business applications have full, centrally tracked visibility into AI agent deployment, access, permissions, ownership and approval. Fewer than half consistently apply common governance controls across all their AI tools and agents.

What to examine: Which AI agent actions require approval, which permissions are restricted, is each action authorized and can every consequential action be traced to an accountable owner?

Excess privileged access goes unchecked

As organizations expand their portfolio of business applications, and adopt AI agents within business applications, foundational access controls become even more important. Yet the survey found that 52% of respondents do not continuously monitor and remediate excess access.

Automation helps teams make access risk management continuous, and it is becoming common across access governance activities. Access controls like segregation of duties (SoD) risk analysis and UARs have been around for quite some time, yet for many organizations manual work remains part of the control equation. When asked to what extent common access governance activities were automated, nearly two-thirds of respondents said each activity was mostly or fully automated. Title: PHP2Shell: What to Expect and What to Do Next
Context: Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why PHP2Shell runs before your app code does, why a clean investigation proves nothing, which secrets to rotate first and how vaulting and just-in-time access limit what a stolen credential can reach.

Roughly seven in ten websites run on PHP. An unpatched PHP server can be broken into with one web request and no password. That hole has been there for 14 years, and attackers reached it before the patch did.

The flaw is PHP2Shell: two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The fix shipped on October 21, 2026, four days after the first exploitation attempts were seen. PHP sits behind 69% of websites whose server-side language is known.

Upgrading PHP is the easy part. The hard part is what attackers already took: database credentials, API keys, session tokens and personal data, each still valid until someone rotates it. Treat every secret the server could read as stolen, including any it fetched from a vault.

A vault with automated rotation makes the cleanup fast. Without one, it is slow, manual work. Either way, rotation fixes the stolen credentials and does nothing about the other two problems. The leaked personal data will fuel targeted phishing and identity attacks for months, and breaches will spread from organizations that patched late to those that depend on them.

This is the first week of a long event.

Four reasons PHP2Shell is more dangerous than a typical critical flaw

Critical web vulnerabilities surface most weeks, and most of them don't deserve the label "dangerous". PHP2Shell does, for four reasons.

1. PHP2Shell runs before your application code does

With Apache mod_php, PHP is embedded in the web server itself. On those servers the exploit fires while PHP is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. PHP-FPM and other setups are affected too, under extra conditions.

The danger: the attack is over before your login page, your multi-factor check or your application's logging is reached. It can succeed and leave no trace where you would normally look.

2. PHP2Shell can leak server memory without leaving a web shell

PHP's advisory for CVE-2026-109619 lists memory disclosure as a confirmed impact. The process that handles requests keeps credentials, tokens and session data from earlier requests in memory, and an attacker can read it without dropping a file or running a command.

The danger: There may be no web shell to find. An investigation that finds nothing has not shown that nothing was taken. Rotate the server's credentials anyway.

3. Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed

Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026. The CVE identifiers leaked on October 20, 2026, so PHP released the fix a day early. Proof-of-concept exploits were circulating hours before the planned release, and Amazon now describes PHP2Shell as broadly exploited in the wild.

The danger: A server patched the day the fix shipped may already have been compromised, and the gap between disclosure and mass exploitation was hours, not days.

4. PHP2Shell has been in PHP since 2012

Calif Research, the firm that found the bugs, traces the earliest affected code path to PHP 5.4.0, released in 2012. A related flaw surfaced in a 2024 audit, but nobody proved it exploitable, so nobody fixed it.

The danger: 14 years of PHP releases are exposed, and more than a third of PHP-powered sites run PHP 7 or older, branches that will never get an official fix. Those servers stay exploitable for months.

A web server is a credential store

Next to the PHP code on a typical server: a config.php with the database password. A .env file with API keys, cloud access keys, mail credentials and OAuth client secrets. Process memory holding the tokens and personal details of whoever was signed in. The PHP process reads all of it, so an attacker whose code runs inside that process can too.

With those secrets, the attacker no longer needs the vulnerability. Every login looks like legitimate traffic, and none of it trips a detection written for the PHP flaw. The vulnerability was the entry. The identities are the payload. A PHP vulnerability becomes an identity problem.

PHP2Shell's aftershocks will come in three waves

This is a forecast, based on how credential theft has played out before.

Wave 1 is now and runs for weeks. Automated exploitation of anything unpatched. Web shells and cryptominers installed. Config files and environment variables harvested at scale. Active sessions hijacked.

Wave 2 starts within a week and continues for months. The harvested credentials are used: database logins from new places, cloud keys to pull data and OAuth secrets to mint tokens for SaaS applications. None of it requires an exploit, and all of it appears to be authorized access.

Wave 3 runs for months or more. Leaked personal data and session details fuel targeted phishing and account takeover against your customers and employees. Some organizations will be breached through a vendor, partner or SaaS provider that ran PHP, patched late and rotated nothing. Their incident becomes yours.

What to do about PHP2Shell, in order

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged immediate patching but, at the time of writing, hasn't listed either CVE as known to be exploited. That is not a reason to wait; the first attempts came before any detection signature existed.

In the next hours. Find every place PHP runs, including appliances that bundle it. Upgrade to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or to your vendor's backported package; there is no complete workaround. Isolate anything you can't patch. Investigate from October 17, not the disclosure date.

In the next days. Assume any secret the server could read is in someone else's hands. Inventory them, rotate them starting with the ones that reach the most systems, and invalidate active sessions. Then audit the systems those credentials open for use you didn't authorize.

In the next months. Change what a web server is allowed to hold. Static secrets in files on an internet-facing host are standing privilege. Move them into a vault that rotates them automatically. Give applications and services just-in-time access scoped to the task, so a stolen credential stops working quickly and reaches only what the task needs. Put phishing-resistant authentication in front of the people who will be targeted. Ask your vendors which of these they've done.

Where identity security does its work

If a credential is stolen, the damage should stop at that credential. The Delinea Platform is built for that outcome; it limits how far an attacker can move and what they can reach if they get in.

Credentials are vaulted and rotated automatically, and in brokered sessions they are injected at the proxy at the moment of use, so database passwords and API keys no longer live in config.php or .env. Access is granted just-in-time, scoped to the task and revoked when it's done. Each privileged action is authorized as it happens and tied to a named identity, so when the board, auditors or regulators ask what happened and why it was allowed, you have an answer.

Patch today, then treat the patch as the beginning. Exploitation started before disclosure, so patching does not mean the attacker is gone, nor does it restore a single credential that was stolen. This is week one. Plan for the year.

Title: Attackers Forge Trust Targeting the Foundations of Identity Trust
Context: The big theme: Attackers are targeting the foundations of identity trust Recent Delinea Labs outlooks have tracked attackers exploiting stolen credentials, third-party...
Full Text:
What you will learn

Find out how forged tokens and exposed signing keys let cyber criminals create trusted identities, why trusted apps and AI agents became entry points, and the four priorities for protecting identity trust in October.

Delinea Labs October 2026 Threat Outlook

In this monthly series, Delinea Labs breaks down the identity-related incidents that had the greatest operational impact over the previous month: how attacks unfolded, what failed in real environments and what those failures signal for the month ahead.

In September, a critical vulnerability in Casdoor exposed a weakness at the core of identity security

An organization administrator could retrieve a private signing key and use it to forge authentication tokens for any user, including global administrators. Rather than stealing an administrator's credentials, an attacker could manufacture an identity the system already trusted.

It was one of several September disclosures pointing to the same problem: weaknesses in the mechanisms that establish and enforce identity trust.

Here's Delinea Labs' outlook for October.

The big theme: Attackers are targeting the foundations of identity trust

Recent Delinea Labs outlooks have tracked attackers exploiting stolen credentials, third-party applications and increasingly autonomous AI agents. September added a new layer: Attackers targeting the systems that decide which identities to trust.

Several vulnerabilities traced back to hard-coded authentication secrets, exposed signing keys, certificate authorities and gaps in authentication or authorization. Any of them could let an attacker forge legitimate-looking tokens, impersonate trusted services or gain privileges beyond their intended scope.

A stolen credential gives an attacker access to an existing identity. A compromised signing key lets them create new ones. Rotating a user's password does little if an attacker can generate another valid authentication token.

As organizations rely more on federated identity, APIs, machine identities and AI agents, the infrastructure that establishes trust needs the same protection as the identities themselves.

What we're seeing at Delinea Labs

Trusted applications became entry points.

Two September incidents showed attackers exploiting access organizations had already granted. At Brevo, a SAML single sign-on (SSO) scoping weakness allowed an attacker to access 138 customer accounts, export contacts from 43 of them, and use 6 of them to send phishing campaigns. Days later, a separate attacker used a long-lived Cloudflare API key stored in source code to deploy malicious code through Brevo-hosted infrastructure.

At BigCommerce, attackers compromised API credentials for third-party Ribon applications, using them to reach merchant environments, steal customer information and inject malicious scripts. BigCommerce said its own platform was not breached.

Access that had been granted to a trusted application turned into a way in

The risk goes up when credentials never expire or permissions cover more than the job requires. Identity verification data is now a tool for attackers.

Identity-verification provider IDScan.net confirmed an unauthorized third party accessed or copied customer information from its cloud platform. The disclosure followed reports that about 153 million driver's-license scans were up for sale. IDScan.net hasn’t confirmed that figure.

Government-issued identification documents are more than sensitive personal information. They’re evidence used to establish identity. Once they’re exposed, attackers can use them for impersonation, social engineering and attempts to get past identity verification.

AI agents keep reaching systems they were never meant to trust. On September 18, Google confirmed Gemini models unintentionally accessed systems belonging to three real companies during cybersecurity evaluations run by Irregular in May. The models were supposed to target fictional organizations. Instead, they had internet access nobody expected, and they used it to discover or guess credentials and authenticate to real systems.

Anthropic identified a fourth incident, in addition to the three covered in last month’s outlook. In January 2026, an early Claude Opus 4.6 model gained unauthorized access to a real third-party system. Anthropic also documented threat actors using AI in intrusion workflows involving credential theft, authentication artifacts and token replay.

AI agents are getting better at finding and using existing access paths on their own. Securing them means controlling not just what they're instructed to do, but which credentials, tools and permissions they can use.

There's a vulnerability here: September recorded 14,841 common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs), including 1,799 identity-related vulnerabilities and 146 affecting identity products, up from 84 in August.

Several disclosures showed how weaknesses in authentication infrastructure can undermine trusted access.

Microsoft Entra ID (CVE-2026-62916 and CVE-2026-83941). Two critical privilege-escalation vulnerabilities affected authentication and authorization controls. One could allow an unauthorized remote attacker to elevate privileges without any existing access; the other could allow an already authorized attacker to gain more. Both are reminders that authentication was only the first check, and what an identity can do afterward still has to be enforced.

Casdoor (CVE-2026-90942 and CVE-2026-91998). One vulnerability exposed an instance-wide signing key that could be used to forge JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) for other users, including global administrators. Another allowed an attacker to use application credentials to manage users across organizations, including creating administrator accounts. Together, they showed how limited access could be transformed into broader authority.

JWT signing-key vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-89026, CVE-2026-85391 and CVE-2026-75431). Vulnerabilities in Issabel, Peppermint and PowerJob came down to hard-coded or predictable signing secrets. Attackers could use them to forge authentication tokens, create unauthorized sessions, and in some cases, achieve remote code execution.

Machine identity forgery (CVE-2026-78234). A vulnerability in hawtio-operator could let users with namespace edit permissions to obtain certificates containing attacker-controlled identity information and use them to impersonate trusted services.

The common thread is clear. Compromising the mechanisms that establish identity can do more damage than compromising a single account.

Ransomware activity

Qilin and TheGentleMen tied for the largest share of September's ransomware activity at 10.66% each, followed by KryBit at 4.96%.

KryBit, a ransomware-as-a-service operation that emerged in March 2026, has expanded across Windows, Linux, VMware ESXi and network-attached storage environments. KryBit reportedly uses phishing and compromised credentials for initial access, which fits the familiar pattern that stolen identities and privileged accounts remain reliable paths from initial compromise to ransomware deployment.

What to prioritize in October

Protect the systems that establish identity trust. Treat JWT signing keys, certificate-authority keys and other signing material as Tier-0 identity assets. Eliminate hard-coded secrets, restrict access and set up reliable rotation and revocation.

Strengthen authorization boundaries. September's Brevo and Entra ID findings showed that authenticating an identity is only the first step. Review federation scoping, cross-organization permissions and privilege-escalation paths, and enforce authorization on the action itself.

Reduce standing privilege for machine and third-party identities. Inventory API keys, service accounts and application integrations. Remove unnecessary permissions and replace long-lived credentials with short-lived, task-scoped access wherever possible.

Enforce AI agent access at runtime. Limit the credentials, tools and network destinations available to agents, and verify their authority when they attempt consequential actions. Model-level restrictions alone can’t contain an agent with access to trusted systems.

A stolen password gives an attacker one identity; a stolen signing key lets them create as many as they want

The Delinea Platform helps organizations discover identities, analyze privilege risk and enforce access control at the moment of action. By extending Privileged Access Management (PAM) from the point of access to the moment of action, organizations can control what AI agents, humans and machines can do, and for how long.

Title: Can Security Controls Keep Up With Fast-Moving AI?
Context: Why identity controls break for AI agents, and how to fix three gaps: attribute every action to the person who launched the agent, replace standing access with just-in-time...
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why identity controls break for AI agents, and how to fix three gaps: attribute every action to the person who launched the agent, replace standing access with just-in-time access and enforce policy in front of key systems.

Consider a common scenario. A platform engineer builds an agent to sort support tickets. The agent reads the ticket queue, looks up customer accounts in the production database and posts summaries in Slack. The engineer connects the agent with an API token from the engineer's own account, because the token already works and the agent can't complete an MFA prompt. The security team approves access once, at setup.

A year later, the engineer has moved to another team. The agent still runs under the engineer's identity with its day-one permissions, and nobody has reviewed its scope. Then a ticket arrives with an instruction buried in the text. The agent follows the instruction, queries a table it was never meant to touch and posts the results back into the ticket. Every log entry points to the engineer, who hasn't worked on the project in months.

Nobody in that scenario was careless. The agent arrived faster than the controls built to govern it could respond. By the time anyone noticed a problem, the agent had been in production for a year, reading tickets, querying customer records and acting under a person's identity.

Agents add to an identity problem that was already growing. Industry estimates of how far non-human identities (NHIs) outnumber people nearly doubled in one year, from 46:1, to 82:1, according to the Delinea 2026 Identity Security Report. In the same report, 46% of organizations admit their identity governance around AI systems is deficient. The question for security leaders isn't whether agents need new controls. The question is which existing controls still hold, and where agents break them.

What still works: Access security fundamentals haven’t changed

The core principles of access security apply to agents the same way they apply to people: least privilege, defined scope, monitoring and approval before access is granted.

An agent with a narrow, documented scope, a named owner and logged actions is a manageable risk, the same as a contractor

Vaulting, least privilege, session recording and approval gates all still work.

What doesn’t hold is what those controls take for granted. Most controls were built around a human pace: a person requests access, someone approves it and a review checks access months later.

An agent is asking for access constantly, so the approval ends up happening once at setup, and then nobody checks it again until the next review. By then the agent has been running for months and has taken thousands of actions no one has reviewed. The support-ticket agent ran for a full year that way.

The controls also count on whatever you provisioned behaving the same way tomorrow as it did today. That assumption holds for service accounts, but not for agents. The same agent with the same permissions will do different things depending on what it reads and who it’s talking to, so the action you approved on Monday might mean something different by Friday. The support-ticket agent behaved as designed for a year, until one ticket changed what the agent did.

Gap 1: Identity controls assume a human is making the decision

Identity and access management (IAM) and multi-factor authentication (MFA) were built around a person: someone logs in, a prompt shows up on their phone, the person decides whether to approve the login. The model depends on a person reading the prompt and making that decision.

Agents behave differently from both people and services accounts, which puts them in their own identity class. An agent can’t complete an MFA prompt, and the developer building the agent usually has a session or an API token that already works, so the agent runs on that token. From then on, every system the agent touches and every action it takes gets recorded under the developer’s identity, with nothing to show that an agent was involved.

The gap surfaces when someone needs answers. An auditor asks who approved the agent’s access to this application, and often nobody can say, because the access was approved for a person and the agent just inherited it. An incident responder finds a command that ran under an employee’s account and can't tell whether the employee or an agent ran the command. In the support-ticket scenario, the responder finds a query against the customer database under the engineer's account, a year after the engineer left the project.

In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 80% of organizations said they can't always understand why an NHI took a privileged action. That number is for service accounts and agents combined.

How do you keep up?

Tie each agent to the person who launched it.

Grant only the access the task needs.

Maintain attribution. Every logged action should show both the agent that took it and the person it acted for.

Gap 2: Access is granted once and rarely reviewed

When an agent is set up, it needs OAuth or API scopes to do its job. Usually those scopes get granted broadly, because nobody knows yet exactly what the agent will need, and granting more access up from is easier than coming back for more. Nobody treats the agent as an account that needs review, so it never enters a review cycle. A year later, the agent still holds its day-one permissions. A person with that much access would have been through several access reviews by then.

Standing privilege is risky for any identity, and the risk is higher for agents. An agent acts on what it reads, so a stray instruction in a ticket or an email can trigger it to use any access it already has. The agent is working as designed. It has no reliable way to tell an instruction it should follow from one it shouldn’t. One instruction hidden in a ticket was enough for the support-ticket agent to query a table it was never meant to touch.

Agents move at machine speed. The gap between something going wrong and the damage being done is usually shorter than anyone’s ability to notice.

Many organizations still depend on standing access. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 59% said they lack a viable alternative to standing access for NHIs and AI agents. Organizations were more than twice as likely to rely on long-lived credentials (35%) as on just-in-time (JIT) access (17%).

How do you keep up?

Remove standing access where the risk is highest.

Grant just-in-time access per task, scoped to what the task needs.

End access automatically when the task is done.

Keep credentials out of the agent’s hands where possible.

Enforce continuous authorization. Place a policy gateway between the agent and the systems an agent reaches, so the gateway evaluates each request against a policy in real time.

Where possible, the credential should stay out of the agent's hands entirely, so the agent has nothing to hold or leak.

Access has to be granted automatically, at the moment the agent needs it, because a process that needs a person to step in each time won't keep pace with an agent. JIT access controls when the agent gets in. Under a continuous authorization model, the gateway then evaluates each request the agent makes against policy and denies the requests outside the scope of the task.

Gap 3: Control can’t wait for discovery

Most organizations can't see all the agents running in their environment. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, more than half of organizations said they regularly find unsanctioned AI tools or agents in their environment, and only 28% said they can detect that activity in real time.

Agents slip past discovery in two ways. Some agents are gone before anything looks for them, because an agent can spin up, act and disappear in minutes, while most organizations take hours or days to detect unsanctioned AI, according to the 2026 Identity Security Report. Other agents run for months and still never appear, because nothing about them was registered. They have no installer, no license record and no product name for a discovery tool to find.

Confidence runs ahead of that reality. In the same report, 82% of organizations said they are confident they can discover NHIs with access to production systems, but only 30% said they validate NHI and agent activity in real time.

A complete inventory would not solve the problem either. Agents appear and disappear daily, so an inventory is out of date the moment it is finished. An inventory also shows which agents exist, not what each agent can reach right now.

Multi-agent systems make the picture harder to trace. Each additional agent adds access paths and handoffs, and when something breaks, tracing the failure back to the agent or step that caused it takes longer with each layer. Long-lived API tokens passed between agents and servers add risk at each hop, whether the connection runs over Model Context Protocol (MCP) or another protocol.

How do you keep up?

Start with the systems that can do the most damage: production database, customer records, deployment pipeline.

Put a policy gateway in front of those systems.

Let gating reveal which agents are trying to reach them.

Keep discovery running in parallel, expanding control as it finds more.

Where the kill switch fits

A lot of the conversation about rogue agents comes down to the emergency shutoff. People want to know who owns it, whether a kill switch at 2 a.m. is already too late and what happens when an agent is holding live credentials at the moment something goes wrong. In most cases, 2 a.m. is too late, because an agent moving at machine speed has usually finished the damage before anyone reaches the switch. In the support-ticket scenario, a kill switch would've stopped the agent only after the results were already posted in the ticket.

Security teams end up asking those questions when the controls upstream didn’t keep up. An agent with no standing credentials, a clear record of whose authority it acted under, and a full log of its actions rarely creates a 2 a.m. emergency.

A common objection is that this slows AI down. In the 2026 Identity Security Report, 90% of organizations said they’re under pressure to loosen access controls to support AI automation. Loosening controls isn't the only path to speed. When controls are already in place, each new agent goes through a process that already exists, instead of starting a new security debate.

Can security controls keep up with fast-moving AI?

The fundamentals can. Least privilege, scoped access and approval still apply to agents. What has to change is when security teams enforce those controls. Under those controls, the support-ticket agent would run under its own identity, linked to the engineer who launched the agent. The agent would receive read access to the ticket queue for each task, and a policy gateway would deny the request for a table outside that task.

Attribution has to follow each agent back to the person who launched it. Access has to be granted per task, not once at setup. Enforcement has to sit in front of the systems that matter, whether or not discovery has found the agent making the request. Controls enforced at the moment of the request can keep pace with an agent. Controls enforced only at setup leave security teams responding after the damage is done.
